bio.en: Scott Belsky is a product legend - founder of Behance (sold to Adobe, where he rose to Chief Product Officer and later Chief Strategy Officer), author of The Messy Middle, and an active angel investor.
bio.zh: Scott Belsky 是一位产品传奇人物——Behance 的创始人（后被 Adobe 收购，他在那里升至首席产品官，后任首席战略官），《混乱的中段》（The Messy Middle）一书的作者，同时也是一位活跃的天使投资人。

summary.en: Scott shares lessons from a career of building and investing, focusing on the 'messy middle' between idea and scale where most of the real work happens. He discusses how to maintain craft and quality amid growth, the role of taste and persistence, and what he looks for in the products and teams he backs. The episode is an inspiring, practitioner's view of what it takes to make enduring products.
summary.zh: Scott 分享了他打造与投资的职业心得，聚焦于介于“想法”与“规模化”之间、绝大多数真正工作发生的“混乱中段（messy middle）”。他讨论了如何在增长中保持工艺与品质、品味与坚持的作用，以及他在押注的产品与团队身上寻找什么。本期是一位实践者对“打造持久产品需要什么”的鼓舞人心的解读。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Yeah. I've had this conversation quite a few times over the years with founders and friends who were running a company going sideways or worse and have had this question, "Should I continue or not?" I always have the same answer. I basically say, "How much conviction do you have in the solution you're building?" I know in the beginning, before you knew all you know now, you had tons of conviction. That's what caused you to leave your job. Now knowing all you know, do you have more or less conviction in the problem and the solution you're building? (00:00:31): And I'll tell you, I get different answers. Some people are like, "Oh, Scott, I mean, I have more conviction. All that I've learned, all the validation I've received from customers, we just haven't figured it out yet. It's driving me crazy. We've tried three times, and it's still like each product fails. But I have more conviction than ever before." And for those people, I'm like, "You know what? You're just in the messy middle. Stick with it. This is par for the course." But oftentimes, I'll hear, "Honestly, if I knew then what I know now, I would not have done this. Holy shit." (00:01:01): I'm like, "Then, quit. Your life is short. You have a great team. Pivot. Do something completely different." If you've lost conviction, you should not be doing what you're doing in the world of entrepreneurship.

是啊，这些年我和很多创业者以及朋友聊过这个话题，他们的公司正面临困境或更糟的境况，总会问：“我该继续下去还是放弃？”我的回答始终如一。我会问：“你对自己正在打造的解决方案还有多少信心？”我知道，在你尚未积累如今这些经验的时候，你曾满怀信心。这份信心甚至促使你辞去原来的工作。如今掌握了更多知识后，你对所面临的问题和解决方案的信心是增强了还是减弱了？  
（00:00:31）说实话，我的答案各不相同。有些人会说：“斯科特，我是说，我的信心更坚定了。我学到了很多东西，客户也给了很多认可，只是我们还没找到正确的方案。这快把我逼疯了。我们已经尝试了三次，每次产品都失败。但我的信心比以往任何时候都更坚定。” 对这些人，我会说：“你知道吗？你正处于混乱的中间阶段。坚持下去。这是创业过程中必经的阶段。” 但更多时候，我会听到：“说实话，如果我现在知道当时所知的那些事，我绝不会这么做。天哪！” 我会回应：“那就退出吧。人生短暂。你有很棒的团队。调整方向。去做完全不同的事情。” 如果你已经失去了信心，那在创业的世界里，你就不该继续做现在这件事了。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Hey, Lenny. And it's great to be here.
turns.zh: 嘿，莱尼。很高兴能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you know this, but it's been a big goal of mine to get you on this podcast since the day I launched it. And so, I'm really excited that you're here. I wanted to start with your role at Adobe. So for the longest time, you're a chief product officer at Adobe. And then recently, I noticed you shifted to this very complicated sounding role. I'm curious what this new role is and then why you made that shift.
turns.zh: 我不知道你是否知道，但自从我创办这个播客以来，让你参与其中就一直是我的一个重要目标。所以你能来这里，我真的很兴奋。我想先从你在Adobe的角色说起。在很长一段时间里，你都是Adobe的首席产品官。最近，我注意到你转到了一个听起来很复杂的新角色。我很好奇这个新角色是什么，以及你为什么会做出这样的转变。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Well, in this new role, I'm overseeing strategy and corporate development, all of design across the company and emerging products for the business. If you look back at the last five years or so, it really has been about getting our core products to the cloud, making them collaborative, making some critical and interesting opportunistic acquisitions over the years, ensuring that we have connectivity between the products that we launched, new web apps that meet new types of creatives. (00:05:49): And that was a incredible five-year-old chapter. Now with the advent of AI and new and emerging fast-growing businesses we have like the 3D and immersive space, the stock business and how that whole space is being changed by new technology, the idea of bringing that into an organization and being able to focus on that full-time was really exciting to me.
turns.zh: 嗯，在这个新角色中，我负责监督公司战略和企业发展、整个公司的设计工作，以及新兴业务产品的开发。回顾过去五年左右的时间，我们的主要工作是将核心产品迁移到云端，使其具备协作功能，多年来进行了几次关键且有趣的收购，确保我们推出的产品之间互联互通，开发满足新型创意需求的网络应用。（00:05:49）这是一个令人惊叹的五年篇章。现在随着人工智能的兴起，以及新兴快速发展的业务领域，比如3D和沉浸式空间、股票业务，以及新技术如何改变整个领域，把这些技术引入组织并能够全职专注于此，对我来说真的很令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is it that you're doing day-to-day now, just even get it even more concrete? I'm curious what your days are looking like.
turns.zh: 那么你现在每天都在做些什么呢？我很好奇你的日常工作是怎样的。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Well, I think that it's the strategy of a company always needs to be iterated. And so being tasked with developing the strategy across the entire company, there's no shortage of opportunities and people to meet and things to think about there. Corporate development, certainly like new M&A stuff and integration, all that sort of stuff falls under me as well. And I have a lot of feelings about that having been an entrepreneur that went through integration myself. So it's kind of fun to be on the other side and try to improve it from that vantage point. (00:06:51): On the design side, I spend a ton of time reviewing the design across every product and really trying to raise the bar for the experiences we're shipping. And that's a hard thing to do in a company that has a lot of legacy products and a lot of baggage that comes with them. And on the emerging products side, it's really about the new products we're bringing into the market and how to make them win.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为公司的战略总是需要不断迭代。因此，负责制定整个公司的战略，肯定有很多机会，可以与不同的人会面并思考各种问题。企业发展方面，像新的并购和整合之类的事情也归我管。这让我很有感触，因为我自己也曾是一名创业者，经历过整合过程。所以站在另一边，试图从这个角度改进现有流程，还是挺有趣的。（00:06:51）在设计方面，我花大量时间审查每个产品的设计，努力提升我们推出的体验水平。在一个有很多遗留产品且背负诸多包袱的公司里，这是一件很难做到的事。在新兴产品方面，就是要把我们推向市场的新产品做好，确保它们能成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that comes up on this podcast a number of times is how CPOs rarely last at a company. They stay. Like Casey mentioned this and a few other people, they stay around for a couple years, and the best they can do is just take a few swings at how things work, improve a few things and then, the CEO's like, "No, this isn't great," and then find someone else. What do you think has contributed to you surviving and lasting and thriving and taking on more and more responsibility at Adobe?
turns.zh: 这个播客中多次提到的一个话题是，首席产品官在公司里通常待不久。他们留任时间不长。比如凯西和其他几个人提到，他们在公司待几年后，最多也就是尝试改进一下现有流程，提升一些地方，然后CEO就会说：“不行，这样不行。”接着就找别人了。你觉得自己能在Adobe生存下来、持续发展并承担越来越多责任的原因是什么？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Well, in the chief product officer role, I oversaw design, product, and engineering. And I think part of the reason I was even interested in coming into the company and taking this role is that I felt like these boundaries between these functions are at best artificial, at worst really constraining. And I always have felt like a lot of products win not because of the technology but the user's experience of the technology. (00:08:08): And so, if you have an aligned team that gets that and makes decisions accordingly, I think you can ship better experiences. So a lot of the work I had to do was breaking some of these boundaries down over the years. And I think that a lot of chief product officer roles traditionally don't oversee engineering and sometimes don't even oversee design. And for me, that wouldn't be interesting.
turns.zh: 嗯，在首席产品官的职位上，我负责设计、产品和工程部门。我认为我有兴趣加入公司并担任这个职位的部分原因在于，我觉得这些职能之间的界限充其量是人为设定的，最坏情况下甚至会带来束缚。我一直认为，很多产品之所以成功，不是因为技术本身，而是用户对技术的体验。（00:08:08）所以，如果你有一个协同一致的团队能理解这一点并据此做出决策，我相信你就能提供更好的用户体验。因此，这些年来我做了很多工作，试图打破这些界限。我注意到，传统上，首席产品官的角色往往不负责工程部门，有时甚至不负责设计部门。但对我来说，这样做毫无意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Zooming into product, if there's a Mount Rushmore of insightful product thinkers, I feel like you'd be on it. And part of the reason is that you have this incredible product sense, whatever that means. It's clear that you have strong product sense. And PMs often talk about the importance of product sense and how to build product sense. And I'm curious, how do you feel like you built your product sense. And what advice would you give to younger PMs looking to build product sense?
turns.zh: 说到产品领域，如果要评选产品思维领域的四大巨头，我觉得你绝对榜上有名。部分原因在于你拥有令人惊叹的产品敏锐度——无论这意味着什么。显然，你确实具备强大的产品敏锐度。产品经理们经常谈论产品敏锐度的重要性，以及如何培养这种敏锐度。我很好奇，你是如何培养自己的产品敏锐度的，又能给那些渴望提升产品敏锐度的年轻产品经理提供哪些建议？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: First of all, I think the biggest mistakes that teams make is they become very passionate about a solution to a problem they're trying to solve as opposed to do everything they can to develop empathy for the customer that's suffering the problem. And oftentimes, the empathy gives you the solution, whereas the passion you have for whatever you think the solution is might be 30 degrees off with the solution actually is. (00:09:20): And so, this development of empathy is a key part of it. And of course, as I think about the discipline of crafting product experiences, to me, it's all about psychology. It's about understanding the natural human tendencies that people have in their most primal moments. I talk a lot about the first mile experiences that we have across any product we use, whether we're a consumer or an enterprise user. In the first 30 seconds of using a new product, you are lazy, vain, and selfish. (00:09:51): You want to get it done super quickly. You want to look good to your colleagues or to your friends. You want to feel successful very quickly by engaging in this product. You don't want to have to watch a tour or read anything, really endure any learning curve whatsoever. (00:10:06): Of course, if you can get people through the first 30 seconds, you have so much opportunity to build a more lasting relationship with that customer and have them understand your mission and the full potential of your product. But we need to ground ourselves with the fact that that's really hard to do. It's fascinating to me that most teams spend the final mile of their time building the product, considering the first mile of the customer's experience using the product. If you can just get more customers through that top of funnel, you are a world-class product team. Let's anchor ourselves on just doing that, and let's use psychology to do so.
turns.zh: 首先，我认为团队最常犯的错误是，他们对试图解决的问题的解决方案过于执着，而非竭尽全力去理解正在遭受该问题的客户的痛点。通常，同理心能为你提供解决方案，而你对自己认为的解决方案的热情，可能与实际的解决方案相差甚远。（00:09:20）因此，培养同理心是关键所在。当然，当我思考产品体验设计的学科时，在我看来，它完全关乎心理学。它关乎理解人们在最原始时刻的自然倾向。我经常谈到我们使用任何产品时的首英里体验，无论是作为消费者还是企业用户。在使用新产品的前30秒，你会感到懒惰、虚荣和自私。（00:09:51）你想尽快完成任务。你想在同事或朋友面前表现出色。你想通过使用这个产品迅速获得成功感。你不想看教程或阅读任何说明，真正忍受任何学习曲线。（00:10:06）当然，如果你能让人们顺利度过前30秒，你就有很多机会与客户建立更持久的关系，让他们理解你的使命和产品的全部潜力。但我们必须承认，这真的很难做到。让我感到惊讶的是，大多数团队把最后一英里的时间花在产品开发上，而忽略了客户使用产品的首英里体验。如果你能让更多客户度过首英里阶段，那你就是世界级的产品团队。让我们专注于做到这一点，并利用心理学来实现这一目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to make sure people understand, when you talk about the first mile, essentially that's the onboarding flow maybe to the activation moment.
turns.zh: 为了确保大家理解，当你谈到首英里时，基本上就是从用户引导流程到激活时刻的过程。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I think that's right. It's the onboarding flow. It's the initial experience. It's the defaults that you see. It's the orientation of where you are. So many products you actually don't exactly know how you got to where you are and how to get home and where to get help. So I would say it's the onboarding. It's the orientation, and it's the defaults.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've been a constant and early advocate of investing in that part of the funnel. And it's interesting how often that comes up on this podcast when people think about how do we improve retention, how do we improve growth. Often, the biggest wins from stories that we get on this podcast are in that part of the flow. And so, another data point to spend more time there. And I wanted to ask you, are you finding even at the stage of Adobe, there's still lots of opportunity in the first mile or do you find that it becomes less and less and less, and then it's less important?
turns.zh: 你一直是早期投资这一环节的坚定支持者。很有趣的是，在这个播客中，当人们思考如何提高用户留存率、促进增长时，经常会提到这一点。我们在播客中听到的成功案例，往往都聚焦于这一环节。因此，这又是一个值得投入更多精力的领域。我想问你，在Adobe这样的公司阶段，是否仍有大量机会，还是说这类机会正逐渐减少，变得不那么重要了？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: The answer is lots of opportunity. The reason is because the customers change. Every new cohort of new customers is different. The new customers you have in the early stages of your product are typically more willing and forgiving customers. And you might nail the onboarding process for them, and then suddenly realize that, "Wait, it's not being as effective anymore." (00:12:02): And the reason is because now you're engaging more of those pragmatist customers, those later stage customers who are initially more skeptical, less forgiving, less willing to deal with your friction. And so, you have to reimagine the onboarding process all over again. I mean when you look at a product like Photoshop, for example, it used to cost hundreds and hundreds of dollars. Now, ow you can get Photoshop for as little as 10 bucks a month. And so of course, the funnel's a lot larger. A Lot more people come in with creative desires without the skills or the tolerance to develop them. And so, that dictates an entire change in the onboarding experience for a product like Photoshop.
turns.zh: 答案是机会依然很多。原因在于客户群体在不断变化。每一批新用户都不同。产品早期阶段的用户通常更容易接受新事物，也更容易原谅产品的不足。你可能为他们成功设计了入门流程，但突然发现效果不再显著。（00:12:02）：因为现在你面对的是更多务实型客户，即更晚期阶段的客户，他们最初更持怀疑态度，更难以容忍摩擦。所以你必须重新构想整个入门流程。比如Photoshop这样的产品，过去售价数百美元，而现在每月只需10美元即可订阅。因此，用户群体规模大得多了。许多没有技能或耐心的人带着创作欲望加入，这就要求Photoshop等产品的入门体验彻底改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It makes me think of something Shishir, the CEO of Coda, shared about how he's like, "I don't really buy this idea of product market fit because you have product market fit with your existing users that love it and know about it, and you always don't have product market fit with the people you want to be used the product." And it's related to what you're talking about. The newest people joining have no idea what you're doing.
turns.zh: 这让我想起Coda的CEO Shishir分享的观点："我不太认同产品与市场契合的观点，因为你与现有用户契合是因为他们了解并喜爱你的产品，而与你希望使用产品的人契合却很难。"这与你讨论的内容不谋而合。新加入的用户根本不明白你在做什么。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I agree with that, and I actually think that the role of AI going forward will be to have applications increasingly meet us where we are. To this day, we've always had to generalize onboarding experiences for the most part for everyone. And I'm really excited about the day when kind of products meet us where we are based on what type of user we are.
turns.zh: 我同意这一观点，而且我认为未来AI的角色将是让应用程序越来越贴近用户的实际情况。到目前为止，我们大多是为所有人设计通用的入门体验。我对未来产品能根据用户类型为我们量身定制体验感到兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a billion AI-related questions for you. So I'm going to hold off just-
turns.zh: 我有无数关于AI的问题想问你。所以我先暂停一下——

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: No problem.
turns.zh: 没关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... a bit. And I wanted to double click on the empathy piece. So you talk about how to become better at product sense. Empathy and understanding the user's problems is really important. Do you have any advice for someone that wants to build that? What can they actually do to become more empathetic and build that part of their skillset?
turns.zh: ……稍等。接下来我想深入探讨同理心部分。你谈到如何提升产品敏锐度，对用户问题的理解和同理心非常重要。对于想要培养这些能力的人，你有什么建议吗？他们可以做些什么来增强同理心并提升这方面的技能？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Well, the most humbling moments for me as a product leader have always been shoulder to shoulder to customers. Watching them actually go about their day, not just use my product but go about their day because what you end up getting is context for a lot of data that you're missing. (00:13:56): When customers are using your product, they're using it amidst everything else around them. In the enterprise, it's all their other meetings and other products and pings that they're getting throughout the day. And as a consumer, it's between dealing with their kids or their loved ones or watching Netflix or whatever the case might be. (00:14:14): And in order to really understand where the customer is and where their mentality is, you have to understand the context in which they're using your product. So part of developing empathy is being shoulder to shoulder and just encountering that reality alongside your customer. And that time, it just gives you better intuition. It helps you understand more. And with empathy, we can then better create quote-unquote, "for ourselves" because by developing empathy for others, we're feeling what they're feeling. We can then be the customer. And, of course, we all know some of the best product customers, some of the best products in the world are made when we are the makers are the customer.
turns.zh: 对我来说，作为产品负责人，最令人谦卑的时刻往往是与客户并肩同行时。看着他们真实地度过每一天——不只是使用我的产品，更是融入日常生活——你最终会获得许多被忽视的数据背景信息。（00:13:56）：当客户使用你的产品时，他们是在与周围的种种事物交织中进行操作。在企业环境中，他们要应对层出不穷的会议、其他产品和各种通知；作为消费者，他们可能需要处理孩子或爱人的事务，或是沉浸于Netflix之类的内容。（00:14:14）：要真正理解客户的处境和心态，你必须了解他们使用产品时的具体场景。因此，培养同理心的一个关键步骤，就是与客户并肩同行，亲身感受他们的真实生活。这种亲身经历能赋予你更敏锐的洞察力，帮助你更深入地理解用户。有了同理心，我们就能更好地为自己创造产品——因为通过理解他人的感受，我们能设身处地为用户着想。当然，我们都知道，世界上许多最出色的产品，都是在创作者同时充当用户的角色时诞生的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It makes me think of Marc Andreessen as this awesome code that I always come back to that everyone's time is already allocated. They don't have time for your product. They're not-
turns.zh: 这让我想起马克·安德森（Marc Andreessen）说过的一句话：每个人的时间都是有限的，他们没有时间去关注你的产品。他们没有时间——

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do I find a new app to [inaudible 00:15:01]
turns.zh: 我该怎么找到一款新应用来[00:15:01未听清]

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: And by the way, as a related note, since I know Lenny, you talk to a lot of guests around product-led growth. And sorry, if I'm skipping around here. But-
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，既然我认识莱尼（Lenny），你经常与许多产品主导增长领域的嘉宾交流。抱歉，如果我在这里跳来跳去了。但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请继续。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: ... I think it's also relevant because everyone's trying to get their products to grow. And the other thing that perplexes me is that product leaders expect people to talk about a product being great. And people don't talk about a product doing exactly what they expected it to do. They talk about a product doing what they didn't expect. (00:15:29): And you look at a product like Tesla. People are not going and talking about how they had a great drive today, but they're talking about the Easter egg they discovered on the dashboard or the cool new feature that they discovered that is associated with Christmas or whatever. (00:15:47): And so, it always is interesting to me. In consumer and even enterprise products maybe especially so, why aren't we optimizing for those things that people wouldn't expect the product to do as a way to get that surprise and delight to talk about it, to develop a relationship with our products? I think that's another piece of the puzzle.
turns.zh: ……我认为这也很重要，因为每个人都在努力让自己的产品增长。另一件让我困惑的事是，产品负责人期望人们谈论产品有多棒。但人们谈论的往往不是产品完全符合预期的东西，而是超出预期的部分。（00:15:29）：以特斯拉为例，人们不会去谈论自己今天开车多棒，而是会谈论在仪表盘上发现的复活节彩蛋，或是发现与圣诞节相关的酷炫新功能。（00:15:47）：所以，这对我来说总是很有趣。无论是在消费者产品中，还是在企业产品中（尤其是后者），我们为什么不优化那些人们意想不到的产品功能呢？这样才能带来惊喜和愉悦，让用户谈论产品，与我们的产品建立更深厚的情感联系。我认为这是拼图的另一块。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting, and reminds me of something I just talked about with Gustav from Spotify whose episode might come out before this or after this about how every great consumer product pulls some kind of magic trick and feels like magic to you, like Spotify as an example. And-
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣，让我想起我刚和Spotify的古斯塔夫（Gustav）讨论过的一个话题。他的那期播客可能在这次对话之前或之后发布，讲的是每个伟大的消费者产品都会玩某种魔术般的把戏，让你感觉神奇。比如Spotify就是一个例子。然后——

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I like that, magic, sort of a little mystery, a little intrigue, a little surprise. It's a classic trick that Hollywood uses all the time. Why don't we use it in our own products?
turns.zh: 我喜欢那种神秘感、悬念感和惊喜感。好莱坞总爱用这种经典套路，可我们自己的产品为什么不借鉴呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let me pull on that thread a little bit about just consumer products in general. You spent a lot of your career, maybe most of your career in consumer, imagine Adobe. There's a lot of B2B elements now as well. And you also angel invest and you help a lot of consumer companies. And tell me if you agree, but it feels like new consumer products basically never work. (00:16:55): And if they do work, there's a period where they work, be real, is going through this now clubhouse. Paparazzi went through this. And then, they fail or fade away. Maybe, they come back and then fade away again. I guess, first of all, do you generally agree that consumer is just so rarely successful in consumer products?
turns.zh: 接下来，我想谈谈消费品领域。你职业生涯的大部分时间可能都在消费品行业，比如Adobe。如今Adobe也涉足B2B领域，同时你还作为天使投资人支持许多消费品公司。说说你的看法吧——新推出的消费品产品似乎很难成功。（00:16:55）即使成功了，也只会维持一阵子，比如Clubhouse和Paparazzi都经历过这种起起落落。有些产品可能会回归，但最终还是消亡了。我觉得，消费品领域成功案例实在太少了。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Uber was a consumer product, but it built a network effect that was never there before. It leveraged excess capacity that was always there, but never tapped. It did something under the hood that gave it lasting power. I think of Pinterest, and I was Ben's first seed angel and product advisor. (00:17:36): And with that product, he had this unique insight into the consumer psychology where it was not as much about getting likes and portraying yourself through pictures of you and seeing pictures of friends and all of this sort of anxiety that is induced by that, but rather helping people collect and represent themselves with their interests. (00:18:03): And so again, that was kind of a new insight that I also think developed its own network effect that enabled it to be lasting. And there was a fascinating business component which was it drove a crapload of traffic to every source of every pin, which then got those sites to then put pin buttons themselves because they wanted more traffic. (00:18:23): So there were underlying things under the hood again that it's sort of tilting the market in his favor. I think that a lot of these other more recent consumer products are just kind of clever momentary interfaces. And they are in effect at the expense of venture capitalists, R&D for the platforms that already have the network effects and already have the distribution channels and the ad sales and everything else. (00:18:50): And so, I think that's why we're seeing B-reels capabilities now also in TikTok, and you're seeing a lot of flashes in the pan, especially in these creative consumer apps, which I've been paying very close attention to. They're fun and novel. But if they really work, those features are then brought into the native Apple camera, for instance.
turns.zh: Uber虽然是消费品，但它构建了前所未有的网络效应。它利用了长期存在却未被开发的闲置产能，深层优化了产品机制。以Pinterest为例，我是本·齐默的首位种子天使投资人兼产品顾问。（00:17:36）他深刻洞察到消费者心理：用户需求并非追逐点赞、炫耀照片或承受社交焦虑，而是通过兴趣标签来表达自我和收集灵感。（00:18:03）这种创新理念催生了网络效应，推动了持续增长。还有个巧妙的商业策略——Pinterest将每个图钉的流量导向源站，促使这些平台自发添加图钉按钮以获取更多流量。（00:18:23）这些底层机制让市场朝着有利方向倾斜。如今许多新消费品只是短暂的潮流玩意儿，实质上是拿风投资金去补贴已有网络效应、分发渠道和广告体系的平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's double click on that. I know this is a big question, but just what have you found is important for a new consumer product to work? You mentioned surprise would be great, network effects, maybe a new insight. What else do you find is important for a durable new consumer product to work?
turns.zh: 再深挖一下这个问题。成功的消费品需要具备哪些关键要素？惊喜感、网络效应、创新洞察力……还有什么？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Yeah. And it's interesting because I think my answer 10 years ago would probably be different than my answer today. I think that there is a nimbleness. And maybe, it started in China with these super apps that were able to do everything. And that changed the idea away from the atomized experiences of a decade plus ago where you wanted a specialized product that did exactly what you wanted in a very reduced way. (00:20:00): I think Snapchat emerged under that world. I think Instagram became valuable to Facebook because of that phenomenon. Fast forward to today where all of us are far more technologically literate and we are able to manage a lot more cognitive load in our everyday technology lifestyles. And so suddenly, we don't mind five tabs. We don't mind features hidden and tucked away in menus because we're sort of used to that now. (00:20:28): And so, maybe that's one of the reasons why these established platforms get away with basically copying any novel new capability as opposed to those becoming apps in and of themselves.
turns.zh: 是的。这很有趣，因为我觉得我十年前的答案可能和今天的不同。我认为现在有一种灵活性。也许这始于中国的超级应用，它们能提供一站式服务。这改变了人们的观念，十年前人们追求的是高度专业化、功能单一的产品。（00:20:00）我认为Snapchat就是在这种背景下兴起的。Instagram也正是因为这种现象才对Facebook产生了价值。快进到今天，我们的技术素养大大提高了，能够在日常科技生活中处理更多信息负荷。所以突然间，我们不介意有五个标签页，也不介意功能隐藏在菜单里，因为我们已经习惯了这种操作。（00:20:28）这或许就是为什么这些成熟平台能随意抄袭新功能，而新应用却难以独立成型的原因之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let me shift a little bit and talk about a tweet that you tweeted about one thing you've learned. You have this amazing thread of just things you have learned over the many years you've been thinking about products and consumer products. And one of them was about how you've learned that, you should do half the things that you want to do, half the features you plan to do, do half the features, offer half the options you want to offer, focus on half the market versus the market you're trying to go after. (00:21:12): Can you just talk about maybe how you came upon that learning and then also just how do you actually do that? It's like, "Sure, great. We're going to do half." But then, which half? And oh, but someone wants this feature so badly, shoot. We can't do them all." So do you have any advice in just how to actually execute that sort of approach?
turns.zh: 接下来我想稍微转换一下话题，谈谈你发的一条推文，内容是关于你学到的一件事。在你多年思考产品和消费品的过程中，积累了大量宝贵的经验。其中，最重要的教训之一就是：你应该只做想做的一半事情，只实现计划的一半功能，只提供想提供的一半选项，只专注于一半市场而非全力开拓新市场。（00:21:12）能否谈谈你是如何获得这个见解的？实际操作起来又该如何执行？比如，“好吧，很棒，我们只做一半功能。”但具体是哪一半呢？哦，可有人特别想要这个功能，真倒霉，我们没法全都实现。”你能否给出一些切实可行的建议，指导我们如何践行这种策略？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I mean one of the first comments I'll just make is whenever I'm asked by teams, what features need to be part of their MVP, how do they decide which features they need to ship first and whatever, I always tell them to optimize for the problems they want to have. You want the problem of customers getting through your funnel, feeling successful, using your product and getting value and then saying to you, "Oh, but I need it on this platform, or I need this capability, or I want to be able to share this." I mean you want those problems. So don't do those features now. (00:22:03): Only do the things that prevent people from getting to the point where they care enough to ask you for anything. Make sure they can get through the signup flow. Make sure they can connect their account. Make sure they can use Google login if they need to, or whatever the case may be. (00:22:16): So I always remind the teams, optimize for the problems you want to have, and make sure that you eliminate all the brick walls, the major catastrophe-type things that can happen. But in terms of the half, the half-half, I learned this the hard way. (00:22:31): When Behance was launching back in 2008, I was always trying to hedge us with product features. I wasn't sure if people would be coming to join groups or if people would be coming for the tip exchange where creatives share best practices with one another, or if people were coming to build their portfolios or just share work in progress. (00:22:54): Maybe, it's too much to build a whole project of your work. Maybe, we can allow people just to share snapshots of their work. And so, we actually launched with pretty much all of these features. And then, it was the most complicated form of Behance, was ironically at the beginning. (00:23:10): And then, what we realized is that some things were taking off, and some things weren't. So I remember when we decided to kill the Tip Exchange. And suddenly, the publishing of projects in the portfolio went up. And we're like, "Oh my gosh. Projects being published is the core metric and it's what drives the traffic back to Behance. Let's do this again. I don't know, let's kill groups." (00:23:33): And so, we killed groups. And lo and behold, more people published more projects. And it was like, "Wow." So actually if you make the whole product about one thing, everyone does that. That core crank operates at 10X the velocity and if that's the most important metric for the business, that's gold. And so, we basically went on a killing spree. And we just started killing things. And over the years, we have actually tried to have this sort of, and I pushed this on many products, things I worked with now whenever you're adding things, consider what you can replace. Consider what you can also remove. (00:24:11): When we updated the portfolio on Behance, I remember we used to have this ability to change the colors of your portfolio in Behance. When people clicked on your profile and saw all your projects, you could control that and add your brand element to it. (00:24:24): And so, we know. We were like, "You know what? What would happen if we just took this away? Would people again focus more on projects?" And so, we took it away. For 24 hours, we had people reaching out to us being like, "Damn you. How could you take away these controls for color of portfolio?" After that 24 hours, we basically never heard about it again. All the portfolios look cleaner and more consistent. And people did the core metric more. And so, I just took from that, try to kill things and everything you think you need to do, you probably only need to do half of it.
turns.zh:
我的意思是，我首先要说的一点是，每当团队问我MVP需要包含哪些功能、如何决定先上线哪些功能等等时，我总是告诉他们，要以用户真正关心的核心问题为导向。用户希望的是能顺利完成注册流程、成功使用产品、获得价值，然后主动向你提出需求，比如“我需要在某个平台上使用这款产品”、“我需要某项功能”、“我希望能分享我的作品”。这些才是你应该关注的核心问题。因此，现在不必急于添加那些无关紧要的功能。

（00:22:03）：首先要确保用户能顺畅完成注册流程、成功关联账户，如果需要可以支持Google登录等功能。（00:22:16）：所以我总是提醒团队，要专注于核心问题，消除所有可能阻碍用户体验的障碍。比如Behance在2008年上线时，我试图用各种功能来规避风险，但不确定用户是会加入小组、参与创意人士互相交流技巧的平台，还是专注于构建作品集或分享在制作品。（00:22:54）：或许建立完整作品集太复杂了，不如先让用户分享作品快照。结果我们把几乎所有功能都上线了，结果最初的Behance版本反而最复杂。（00:23:10）：后来我们发现有些功能火爆，有些则冷落。例如决定关闭Tip Exchange功能后，项目发布量激增。我们重新启用项目发布功能，发现效果更好。（00:23:33）：于是我们关闭了小组功能，用户发布的项目数量再次攀升。这启发我们：如果整个产品围绕一个核心功能打造，每个人都会专注于此。核心功能的效率会提升十倍，如果这是业务最重要的指标，那就是成功之道。于是我们开始大胆删减功能。多年来，我在多个产品中推广这个理念：每次添加新功能时，都要考虑替代或移除现有功能。（00:24:11）：比如Behance的作品集更新功能，用户曾能自定义作品集颜色。点击个人资料查看项目时，用户可以控制颜色并添加品牌元素。我们测试发现，如果去掉这项功能，用户会更专注于项目本身。于是我们将其移除。24小时内，用户不断反馈“你们怎么能取消这个功能？”。24小时后，作品集更加整洁一致，核心指标显著提升。从中我领悟到：大胆删减功能，专注核心，用户自然会更投入。
需要做的事，你可能只需要做一半就够了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wonder if in reality most of the time, you only realize this afterwards versus ahead of time. And that's just the way it is. And then, it's just the seal of sunset, things that aren't actually important.
turns.zh: 我想知道，在现实生活中，大多数时候人们往往是事后才意识到这一点，而不是事先就察觉到的。而这就是生活的常态。然后，日落的余晖也好，那些看似无关紧要的事情也罢，都不过是过眼云烟。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I do have to say though, Lenny, some of the best product leaders that I've worked with, I do feel like they have this great reductionist or minimalistic tendency by default. They're just very much... They anchor themselves on the one thing they want people to do and do well. And they just are pretty ruthless about everything else, being like, "Okay, but only if we have a problem with doing this core thing. Okay, put on the back burner." And so, it's something I've tried to get better at over the years.
turns.zh: 不过我得说，莱尼，我合作过的一些最优秀的产品负责人确实天生就具有简化主义或极简主义的倾向。他们专注于让用户做好一件事，其他事情则一律从简。遇到核心任务无法推进时，他们会毫不犹豫地搁置其他事项，说：“好吧，但只有在核心任务出现问题时才考虑这些。先放一放。” 多年来，我一直努力向他们看齐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's really interesting is this is exactly like Matt Mochary who is actually the number one most popular podcast episode talks about when you let people go. And he's helped a lot of CEOs let people go that 100% of the time everything just starts moving faster as soon as you have fewer people. And so, it's the same exact model in people and products.
turns.zh: 真正有趣的是，这和马特·莫查里（Matt Mochary）在播客中谈到的裁员策略如出一辙。他帮助过许多CEO裁员，结果发现只要裁员人数减少，事情往往会进展得更快。这在人力管理和产品开发上都是同样的模式。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I think that's right. And that's why I always feel like tough decisions almost always afterwards feel like a relief. And that's true for the product. That's true for people on a team as well.
turns.zh: 我觉得这没错。这就是为什么我总觉得艰难的决策在事后往往让人如释重负。无论是对产品，还是对团队成员都是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's shift to talking about AI, which I'm really excited about because I know you've been spending a lot of time talking with people about AI, building AI products. You all launched Firefly, which a lot of people are really excited about. You also have this newsletter where you kind of just share your implications on how AI and technology is going to impact the world. (00:26:33): So I have a lot of questions I'm excited to ask you around this. And I'll just start really broad and maybe this is too big of a question, but just how different do you expect the world to be in, say, five years as a result of AI, both for product builders and then just people in general?
turns.zh: 接下来聊聊AI吧。我对这个领域特别感兴趣，因为我知道你花了很多时间与人探讨AI技术，开发AI产品。你们推出了备受瞩目的Firefly产品，还开通了每周通讯，分享AI和科技将如何影响世界的洞见。（00:26:33）：关于这个话题，我有很多问题想请教你。我先抛个大问题，五年后，在AI的影响下，无论是对产品开发者，还是对普通人，世界会变得有多么不同？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Listen, I'm an optimist. And I feel like our human potential has always been held back by the laws of physics essentially. The mundane, repetitive labor you need to do to get anything done is what holds back our ingenuity. It's the friction. It's the work in workflows that wouldn't it be great if we could just have flow and no work? (00:27:15): And I think that that's what AI kind of does, is it gets us from workflow to flow. It gets us into this flow state where any idea in your mind's eye, you can start to develop it. I was having this discussion with Howie who runs Airtable actually just earlier today where we were talking about the leader at IBM who announced that he's not going to hire 8,000 people that he would've hired because AI is going to be able to do that work. (00:27:46): And what we were talking about was, and how he made the point, as engineers have become much more productive over the years, that doesn't mean that companies have wanted fewer engineers. It actually just means that they demand more of their engineers. And engineers have more possibility to do more. (00:28:02): And so, if human ingenuity goes up, maybe we actually want to hire more people because if you have more ingenuity per human being, maybe you can actually do more as a company. And maybe, companies that used to have three products will have five products or seven products or 30 products. And maybe, that's actually the trend that we're forgetting is that humans bring this level of ingenuity to every problem and every opportunity. Whereas computers remember like ChatGPT is basically just giving you what it would look like if, right? It's not truly finding edges that will become the center. (00:28:38): It's actually just mining the center. And it's trying to regurgitate the center, which is also very helpful by the way. So I'm optimistic. I think that there will be far more people engaged in delivering experiences. I'm very long the experience economy because I think that there will be some people liberated to focus more on the non-scalable things that really move the needle for experiences for customers. And then, I also am excited about humans having less grudge work to do.
turns.zh:
听着，我是个乐观主义者。我觉得人类的潜力一直被物理定律所束缚。为了完成任何任务，你需要做那些平凡、重复的劳动，这正是抑制我们创造力的阻碍。这是摩擦力。这是工作流程中的阻碍——如果我们能让工作流程顺畅，没有阻碍，那不是很棒吗？（00:27:15）：我认为AI正是做到了这一点，让我们从工作流程转向顺畅的状态。只要你脑海中有了想法，就能开始开发它。今天早些时候，我和Airtable的Howie讨论这个问题时，他提到了IBM的领导层宣布，由于AI能够接手相关工作，公司将不再招聘8000名员工。（00:27:46）：我们探讨了这个问题，工程师们近年来的生产力显著提升，但这并不意味着公司需要更少的工程师。相反，公司对工程师的要求更高了。工程师有更多可能创造更多价值。（00:28:02）：所以，如果人类的创造力提升，或许我们反而会招聘更多员工，因为每位人类创造力的提升，意味着公司能创造更多价值。那些曾经只有三款产品的公司，或许会推出五款、七款甚至30款产品。也许我们忽视了一个趋势——人类为每个问题和机遇注入创造力。而像ChatGPT这样的AI工具，基本上只是呈现出某种可能性，对吧？它并不能真正找到能成为核心的突破点。
（00:28:38）：它实际上只是挖掘已有的核心答案。虽然这样做也很有帮助。总之，我很乐观。我认为将有更多人投身于提供优质体验的工作。我看好体验经济，因为我相信会有更多人从可扩展性不强的、但对客户体验至关重要的非标准化工作中解放出来，专注于创新。另外，我也很期待人类能减少重复性工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm also excited for that. It reminds me it might have a TikTok account, and I have this team that helps with the TikTok and we haven't shared this, but a few of the TikToks are my voice generated with AI. And they just-
turns.zh: 我也为此感到兴奋。这让我想起它可能有个TikTok账号，我有一个团队负责TikTok相关事务，虽然我们还没分享过，但有几个TikTok视频是用AI生成的我的声音。它们听起来

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... read script. And it's me reading this story. And it sounds sort of like me. And I showed it to a friend. And I was like, "Do you see anything? You feel weird about this video?" And he is like, "No, you sound great. You sound really a great speaker." I'm like, "Okay. Say hi."
turns.zh: ……读剧本。是我在讲述这个故事。听起来很像我本人。然后我把视频展示给一个朋友，他说：“你看到什么了吗？对这个视频有什么感觉？”我说：“没啊，你听起来很棒，是个很棒的演讲者。”他说：“好吧，说句话吧。”

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: While you were reading, instead of reading a script, you can be plotting the course of the next episode.
turns.zh: 当你在阅读时，与其读剧本，不如规划下一集的路线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So I totally see what you're talking about there. In the product team, which function do you think will be the most disrupted and/or the most, I don't know, optimized through AI?
turns.zh: 是的，完全明白你的意思。在产品团队中，你认为哪个职能部门会受到AI的冲击最大/或者最有可能通过AI得到优化？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: We're entering the era where we collapse the stack in every organization where instead of having to go to someone for anything, you can kind of do more things yourself. It's very empowering to get the answer from data as opposed to having to go to a data scientist or a data analyst in the middle. (00:30:12): So there's going to be far less game of operator across the organization and far more empowerment for people to dig their own rabbit holes, answer their own questions and get things done. (00:30:24): I happen to believe that that's the advantage typically of small teams, is that they're flat. The stack is collapsed. People all can hear each other in an audible across the room, and that's how they run circles around big stodgy old companies that are dispersed around the world. So maybe, this technology allows cross-functional work and to happen. And I'm excited about that.
turns.zh: 我们正步入一个组织中数据栈被扁平化的时代——不再需要为任何事情找人求助，你可以自己完成更多工作。从数据中获取答案，而非依赖数据科学家或数据分析师，这种方式极具赋能性。（00:30:12）：因此，组织内的“操作员博弈”将大大减少，人们将有更多机会深入探索、自主解答问题并高效完成任务。（00:30:24）：我认为小团队的优势通常在于扁平化结构。数据栈被打通，团队成员能在办公室里随时交流，这正是他们能绕过那些分散在全球各地、动作迟缓的传统大企业的关键所在。或许，这项技术能实现跨职能协作，我对此充满期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. So essentially, what you're saying is a PM will be able to do more design, more engineering, more data potentially. And maybe, one day, it'll be just as good as having a data scientist in your team. But essentially, everyone becomes kind of this unicorn cross-functional mini-team,
turns.zh: 这确实很有趣。所以你的意思是，产品经理将能够承担更多设计、工程和数据相关的工作？或许有一天，他们的能力甚至能与数据科学家相媲美。但本质上，每个人都将成为这种跨职能的迷你超级团队，

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Which sort of suggests this idea of meritocracy. It's almost like what if people get promoted an opportunity based on how creative and how much ingenuity they have as opposed to how many reports or bug things they've gone through or whatever else. So there's something about what you're saying that I do think, yes, it's disruptive to the degree that, well, you need a data analyst in the loop. But I also would suggest that again, that data analyst doesn't have to answer redundant requests all day. She can spend time on thinking of other things without the boundaries of functions like we just discussed.
turns.zh: 这在某种程度上暗示了精英管理理念。如果人们能基于创造力和创新能力而非处理过多报告或修复bug等传统标准获得晋升机会，那会怎样？所以你所说的内容确实具有颠覆性——毕竟传统模式下确实需要数据分析师参与。但我也要指出，数据分析师不必整天处理重复请求。他们可以专注于思考其他问题，而无需受限于我们刚刚讨论的职能边界。

turns.en: This episode is brought to you by rows.com. The world runs on spreadsheets. You probably have a tab open with a spreadsheet right now. But the spreadsheet product you're using today was designed decades ago. And it shows, they live in silos away from your business data. They weren't made to be used on a phone. And if you want to do even the simplest automation, you have to figure out complex scripts that are nightmare to maintain. (00:32:05): Rows is different. It combines a modern spreadsheet editor, data integrations with APIs and your business tools and a slick sharing experience that turns any spreadsheet into a beautiful interactive website that you'll be proud to share. If you're writing a report on a growth experiment, you can use Rows to do your analysis on data straight from BigQuery or Snowflake. If you're deep diving on marketing, you can import reports straight from Google Analytics, Facebook Ads, or Twitter, or if you're working with sales, you can natively plug Stripe, Salesforce or HubSpot directly into Rows. (00:32:36): And when you're done, you can share your work as a beautiful spreadsheet that's easy to read and embed charts, tables and calculators into Notion Confluence or anywhere on the web. I've already moved some of my favorite spreadsheet templates to Rows. Go to rows.com/lenny to check them out. That's rows.com/lenny. A lot of listeners are product managers. And so just going a little bit further, even within the product management function, how do you see the PM role changing in the next five years as a result of AI?
