turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Well, let me start by saying that I think that the greatest performers I've ever worked with, whether they're designers or product leaders, basically preserve the time to explore lots of possibilities. They call those possibilities down to fewer set. They get feedback on those. They refine them even further. (00:33:24): And then, they present to the team. These are the two or three things I think we should do. And that's the way a great designer works, for example. That is a function of time. If you have the skills and the capabilities, it's just how much time. How much time do you have to explore the full surface area of possibility and find the best possible option. (00:33:43): In my world, in my mind, generative AI and AI for all, when it talks to me about just product leaders exploring possibilities, this should expand the surface area. I was talking to a pretty well known director in Hollywood world, and he was telling me that he uses ChatGPT. I was like, "No. Are you serious? You do?" (00:34:04): And he was like, "Yeah, I don't use it to write any scripts." But sometimes when I'm developing something with a writing partner, I will ask ChatGPT, "What would you do?" And I'll explain the full instance, the full situation in extreme detail. And it will spit out five scenarios. And I actually don't use any of them, but it just gives me more surface area. It tells me the things that I wouldn't want to do, which is also good data. And I just thought that response is so interesting. And so when you ask about product leaders, I think that's what we're going to have, is we're going to have the superpower of exploring far more surface area in far less time.
turns.zh: 好，我先说一下，我认为我合作过的最优秀的从业者，无论是设计师还是产品负责人，他们都会留出足够的时间去探索各种可能性，将这些可能性缩减至可行的范围，收集反馈并进一步完善。（00:33:24）然后向团队展示："这两三个点是我们应该优先推进的。"这就是优秀设计师的工作方式。这完全取决于时间的分配——如果你具备相应技能和能力，最关键的还是时间投入。需要多少时间去探索所有可能性，再从中筛选出最优方案？（00:33:43）在我的认知里，生成式人工智能和普惠型人工智能（AI for All）本质上都是为产品负责人探索可能性而服务的，但生成式人工智能应该能极大扩展可能性边界。比如，我曾与一位好莱坞知名导演交流，他告诉我自己使用ChatGPT。我当时惊讶地问："真的吗？你确定？"他回答："是的，我不会用它写剧本，但有时和编剧合作时，我会问ChatGPT‘你会怎么做？’然后详细描述整个场景和情境，它会输出五种方案。虽然我最终不会采用其中任何一个，但这种多元思维极大丰富了我的思路，让我能识别出不可行的方案，这些反馈同样宝贵。这种对话方式真的很有趣。所以谈到产品负责人，我们需要赋予他们在更短时间内探索更多可能性的超能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of something I always share about why do you need a PM? Why do you need a designer? Why do you need a researcher? It's not necessarily that they're just very good at these specific skills. It's that they just have time to do this one thing that needs to be done. You can have engineers do the PM role, but they don't have time. They want to code and they'd rather do that. And so, this is really interesting that it connects to. It'll give everyone a little more time to get better at the thing they want to be doing.
turns.zh: 这让我想起我常分享的一个观点：为什么需要产品经理？为什么需要设计师？为什么需要研究员？不一定是因为他们擅长某项技能，而是因为他们有时间专注于需要完成的任务。工程师可以兼任产品经理，但他们没有时间。他们更想写代码。这次对话让我意识到两者的关联。它能为每个人争取更多时间，让他们专注于自己想做的事。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: That's true.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you're doing with PMs at Adobe at this point that help them leverage these tools and just the ways of working that you're actually using today?
turns.zh: 目前Adobe在产品经理培训方面有什么举措，能帮助他们更好地利用这些工具和现有工作方式吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: One of my obsessions has been bringing design earlier into the process of product development. So it's not necessarily AI yet. But it's the idea of designers, first of all, being in the room, even being in the room with some of the customer research and some of the debates around even the value proposition to the customer and some of the things that traditionally happen only with the PMs. I just find that, again, collapsing the stack, if you will. Having the designer hear these things and contribute gives them a golden gut as they are then sitting down later and going through possible interfaces to solve the problem. (00:35:57): So I love bringing design upstream. In fact, that's probably been the cheat code of my career as a product leader, has just been disproportionately empowering design throughout the process. I think what we're going to start seeing is generative AI augmenting the designer's work in real time. (00:36:15): So right now, I mean in Photoshop, we're experimenting with instead of just reducing an image and cropping, you can also extend an image. And that's, of course, using generative AI for out painting. And so, you can imagine as you're doing edits in that as well as in other forms of design, getting kind of thumbnails of what you might be trying to accomplish and then touching them, almost like predictive text to go to the next step, to the next step, to the next step and take leaps in the creative process as opposed to incremental steps. (00:36:47): I think that that's going to happen far more. And hopefully, product designers, product managers will be involved to some extent in some of these decision points as designers have more options to choose from.
turns.zh:
我的一个执念，就是要让设计在产品开发过程中更早介入。虽然目前还不是人工智能阶段，但核心理念是，首先让设计师参与到整个过程中，甚至参与客户调研、围绕客户价值主张展开讨论等传统上由产品经理负责的工作。这样一来，设计师就能在后续设计可能的解决方案界面时，获得更深刻的洞察。（00:35:57）所以我热衷于将设计环节前置。事实上，这或许是我作为产品负责人的职业秘籍——在整个过程中不成比例地赋予设计团队权力。未来我们将见证生成式AI实时助力设计师的工作。

（00:36:15）比如在Photoshop中，我们正在尝试的功能不再是单纯的图像裁剪和缩放，而是可以扩展图像。这当然是利用生成式AI进行填充。可以想象，在编辑过程中以及其他设计场景中，用户能获得所需实现效果的缩略图，然后通过类似预测文本的交互方式，快速推进到下一步，推动创意进程而非渐进式改进。

（00:36:47）我相信这种趋势会越来越普及。希望产品设计师和产品经理能在某些决策节点上参与其中，因为设计师将拥有更多选择空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You threw out this term golden gut. What is that about?
turns.zh: 你提到了“金点子”这个术语，能解释一下吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: The golden gut is when you're designing an experience and a flow. You are playing around with all kinds of options. You're moving things around. You're saying, "Actually, that's too complicated. Maybe I'll separate this one page into three steps as opposed to one page with three steps in a row. How do I break this down? How do I simplify?" (00:37:26): You sometimes have instincts like, "Well wait, what if I just remove this all together? What if you didn't even have this whole series of steps? What if I just had a presumptuous default instead and customers could change it if they think they need to?" (00:37:39): And in some of those sorts of, I wonder if, I wonder if, I wonder if, to me is the difference between a very junior product thinker and a very experienced product thinker? I think experienced product thinkers with that golden gut of, "Oh my gosh. Wait, reduction of cognitive load." Maybe even if 10% of people get confused to get 90% of people far faster through this process is a big win and a great opportunity cost trade off. I think those sorts of little micro-decisions that we make in the process of building products, that's the golden gut.
turns.zh:
“金点子”指的是在设计体验和流程时，反复尝试各种方案。调整元素位置，思考：“这样太复杂了，或许我该把这一页拆分成三步而非一页连环步骤。如何简化？如何拆解？”
（00:37:26）有时会有直觉：“等等，如果我把这部分完全去掉呢？如果没有这套步骤呢？如果默认采用一个预设选项，用户可以根据需求调整呢？”
（00:37:39）在这些微观决策中，经验丰富的产品设计师是否能预见问题？我认为这就是初级产品思维者和资深产品思维者的区别所在。资深者凭借“天哪，减少认知负荷”的金点子，即使10%的人会感到困惑，但让90%的人更快完成任务，也是巨大的胜算和机会成本交换。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. I have not heard that term before. For PMs listening and they're like, "Okay, AI's happening. I don't know what to do," what would be your advice for them to stay ahead and be aware of where things are going and not be left behind?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个术语。以前从未听过。对于听众中的产品经理来说，如果他们感到“AI来了，我不知道该做什么”，您有什么建议帮助他们保持领先、把握趋势、避免被淘汰？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Quite simply in one word, play. We all have to be playing with this technology. We have to find ways. The risk of becoming more experienced in your career is you get stuck in your ways. And you're like, "Ah, no. I don't need to have that automatic draft in my email and get ChatGPT to suggest what I want to respond with. I'm fine without that." Make sure you try it. Make sure you play with it. Write poems for your friends. Try a lot of these various generative AI tools out there just to see what's possible and pursue every curiosity. (00:39:06): The reason I started the Implications newsletters is because I was seeing this high velocity of new stuff every day. And I'm like, "I have to force myself to make sure I understand all of this and think about how these implications will change my business as well as the world that I operate in." And there was no better way to do that than to have to write about it, and promise my readers I'll get a monthly thing out there. So I just think we all have to do some version of that.
turns.zh:
简而言之，就一个词——实践。我们都需要用这项技术去玩味它。我们必须想办法突破固有思维。若你深陷职业倦怠，可能会说：“啊，不用，我不需要邮件自动回复功能，也不让ChatGPT帮我构思回复内容。这些功能对我没用。”但一定要亲自尝试，尽情玩味。给朋友写首诗，试用市面上各种生成式AI工具，看看能创造出什么惊喜，满足每个好奇心。

（00:39:06）我创办《影响力》新闻通讯的原因，是因为每天新技术层出不穷。我想：“我必须强迫自己理解这一切，思考这些影响将如何改变我的业务和所处的世界。” 最好的学习方式就是写作，并向读者承诺每月推出新内容。所以我认为，我们都应该尝试类似的做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's plug Implications while we're at it. How do people go subscribe or do they find it?
turns.zh: 顺便宣传一下《影响力》吧。人们怎么订阅或者找到它呢？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Yeah. No. It's implications.com. So it's easy to find, but it's a monthly exercise where throughout the month, I try to capture a few things I think are important. And I really try to go deep down the rabbit hole of what the implications are for various parts of our work and life. And it's been a fun exercise. And also, I get some good polarizing feedback in the process.
turns.zh: 对。网址是implications.com。很容易找到的。这份月刊的核心在于，我每月都会捕捉一些我认为重要的事物，深入探讨它们对我们工作和生活各方面的影响。这是一次很有趣的尝试。过程中我也收到过一些很有争议的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh you do? Interesting. You should share that. That'd be interesting, is here's what I'm getting in response to the stuff I'm writing. This also touches on a thread that comes up a lot on this podcast, is the power of just writing to help you think through stuff. A lot of people think my newsletters, I'm just sharing all these things I know. I'm just like, "I know it in my head. I'm just going to share it in the thing." But it's more. The writing helps me figure it out and gives me an excuse. And like you said, it's a forcing function to spend the time crystallizing it. And so, that's another reminder for that.
turns.zh: 哦，是吗？有意思。你应该分享一下。看看读者对你的内容有什么反应，这也很有意思。这也触及了我们播客中常提的一个话题——写作能帮助你理清思路。很多人以为我的通讯就是分享已知知识，但不止于此。写作能帮助我理清思路，也给了我一个强制执行的理由。正如你所说，这是一种迫使自己花时间把事情想清楚的机制。这也再次提醒了我们这一点。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: And capturing those things, I think, the thing I've kind of learned over the years with writing and also with product development is sometimes you capture these little glimpses and things or sketches, and they become relevant years later. So don't always capture and write because of a foreseeable need for that content. Consider it almost like a back burner that you're constantly tending to. And imagine that three years from now, the stars will align, and this will become invaluable content or some crucial idea for a problem you're facing at the moment.
turns.zh: 关于捕捉这些想法，我认为通过多年写作和产品开发的经验，我学会了有时候捕捉这些小灵感、草图或片段，几年后它们会变得非常有用。因此，不必因为预期需要这些内容才去捕捉和写作。可以把它视为一个需要持续打理的后备项目。想象一下，三年后条件成熟了，这些内容会成为无价之宝，或成为你当前面临的某个问题的关键思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of people actually in your shoes that want to write more and put content out, but that also have a full-time job with a lot of things on your plate. Any advice for actually getting it done the way you've been getting it done?
turns.zh: 实际上，有很多人和你处境相似，想要多写作、多输出内容，但又要兼顾全职工作。对于如何像你一样坚持下去，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Listen, there's no hack to it other than ruthlessness of time and prioritization saying no to most things. This morning, I went for a run and I was like, "I have 40 minutes exactly until I have to get in the shower and I have to be somewhere in 30 minutes from that moment." I'm going to take those 40 minutes or at least 35 of them, and I'm going to write. I don't care if I write five words or five pages. And it's just a great... Without that discipline though, as you said, it's super hard to get it in the seams of the schedule.
turns.zh: 听着，这个秘诀无非是时间的无情和优先级管理——学会对大多数事情说“不”。今天早上我去跑步时，心里想：“距离必须洗澡还有整整40分钟，而从那时起30分钟后我就得去某个地方。”我要利用这40分钟，或者至少35分钟，写作。即便只写五个字或五页字，我也无所谓。这种感觉太棒了……但正如你所说，没有这种自律，要想在日程中挤出时间实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of discipline, you wrote a book called The Messy Middle. And without even talking about what it is, title's pretty... I think people feel like, "I get it." And imagine many people listening are founders or PMs that are feeling like they're in this messy middle. What is one piece of advice for people in this period that you think might help them through the messy middle?
turns.zh: 说到自律，你写了一本叫《混乱的中期》的书。先不谈书名本身，这个标题就很吸引人……我觉得人们会感叹：“我懂了。” 想象一下，许多听众是创业者或产品经理，他们正身处这个混乱的中期阶段。对于处在这一时期的人，你有什么建议能帮助他们度过这段艰难时期？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: The bottom line is that these years in the middle of whether it's a venture, [inaudible 00:42:19] new startup, old turnaround within a big company, they are messy because they are full of lows. It's very volatile. When you're in those lows, you need to find a way to endure them. You need to endure the anonymity and uncertainty and anxiety. (00:42:32): I'm sure a lot of listeners, whether they're in big companies or starting their own company, it's hard to be doing something that no one knows or cares about. And I always like to remind myself that the life expectancy of humans a hundred plus years ago was 25 years old. So the idea of spending three to five years of your life on something, especially if it might fail, was a bad decision. And I think biologically, we feel the need for constant rewards and affirmation to stick with something long enough. (00:43:01): And in fact, most of your listeners were all building things that take many, many years to defy the odds. And we have to overcome our natural human tendencies in this instance by sticking together long enough to figure it out. So how do you do that? (00:43:16): I mean, obviously, part of it is culture, wanting to serve the customers you serve and working with the team you are working with and that being enough to kind of stick it long enough. I think part of it is short-circuiting the reward system, finding micro goals and milestones that are mutually agreed upon. We're going to celebrate these even though in the greater scheme of things, they don't matter much. (00:43:39): I think that's a key part of keeping the team and keeping the dream alive. I always like to use the analogy of we're driving our teams across country as product leaders with the windows blacked out in the backseat and everyone's sitting in the backseat. And so, if they don't know what we're doing that we're making progress, this traffic is clearing, we just cross state lines. If they don't receive the narrative, they will go stir-crazy. And so there's a lot of research around progress, be getting progress and how progress is a source of motivation. And so as product leaders, we have to merchandise progress. We have to be the steward of this narrative.
turns.zh: 关键在于，这些年——无论是创业公司、新创企业，还是大公司内部的转型项目——都充满低谷，因此显得混乱不堪。局势极不稳定。当你身处低谷时，必须找到忍耐的力量。必须承受被忽视、面对不确定性和焦虑的煎熬。（00:42:32）：我相信许多听众，无论是在大公司还是自主创业，都很难从事那些无人问津或无人关心的项目。我总是提醒自己，100多年前人类的平均寿命只有25岁。因此，花三到五年时间在某件事上，尤其是可能失败的项目上，本就是个糟糕的决定。从生物学角度来看，我们天生需要不断获得回报和认可，才能坚持下去。（00:43:01）：事实上，你的大多数听众都在从事需要多年时间才能突破重围的项目。在这种情况下，我们必须克服人性弱点，坚持足够久才能找到出路。那么该如何做到呢？（00:43:16）：显然，部分在于文化——致力于服务客户，与团队共同奋斗，这些就足以支撑我们坚持下去。另一部分在于短路奖励机制，找到双方认同的微目标和里程碑。即使这些在大局中微不足道，我们也要庆祝它们的达成。（00:43:39）：我认为这是维系团队和梦想的重要手段。我常用一个比喻：作为产品负责人，我们要像驾驶团队穿越国境的司机，后排车窗被遮住，所有人坐在后排。如果他们不知道我们在前进，交通在疏通，州界即将跨越。如果他们得不到信息反馈，就会陷入焦虑。因此，关于进展的研究很多，进展本身就是一种激励源泉。作为产品负责人，我们必须包装好进展，充当这个叙事的守护者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you touched on this a bit as you were just talking, but there's also this moment where it makes sense to quit like you shouldn't stay with things endlessly. And I guess any advice on just when something is like, "Okay, you should probably move on from this." Makes me think a little bit about there's all these companies that just keep going that maybe shouldn't keep going because they have enough money or they're just like, "No, founders never quit." Any advice or thoughts that you share there?
turns.zh: 刚才你提到这个问题时已经稍微谈到了，但确实有那么一个时刻，人们会意识到是时候放手了。你觉得什么时候应该停止？这让我想起很多公司在运营不善时继续坚持下去，或许本不该这样做，因为他们有足够的资金，或者只是觉得“创始人永远不应放弃”。你对此有什么建议或看法吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Yeah. I've had this conversation quite a few times over the years with founders and friends who were running a company going sideways or worse and have had this question, "Should I continue or not?" I always have the same answer. I basically say, and I really ask, "How much conviction do you have in the solution you're building?" (00:45:12): I know in the beginning before you knew all know, you had tons of conviction. That's what caused you to leave your job. That's what caused you to take all this risk and hire people and raise money and all this stuff. Now, knowing all you know, do you have more or less conviction in the problem and the solution you're building? And I'll tell you, I get different answers. So some people are like, "Oh, Scott, I mean I have more conviction. All that I've learned, all the validation I've received from customers, we just haven't figured it out yet. It's driving me crazy. We've tried three times, and it's still like each product fails, but I have more conviction than ever before." (00:45:49): And for those people, I'm like, "You know what? You're just in the messy middle. Stick with it. This is par for the course." But oftentimes, I'll hear, "Honestly, if I knew then what I know now, I would not have done this. Holy shit. " I'm like, "Then quit." Your life is short. You have a great team. Pivot. Do something completely different. If you've lost conviction, you should not be doing what you're doing in the world of entrepreneurship.
turns.zh: 是的。这些年我和很多创业者及朋友聊过这个话题，他们的公司正面临困境或更糟的境况，总会问：“我该继续还是放弃？”我的回答始终如一。我会问：“你对自己正在打造的解决方案还有多大的信念？”（00:45:12）：我知道在你还一无所知的时候，你曾满怀信念。这促使你辞去工作，冒险创业，招募团队、融资等等。而现在，了解了所有背景信息后，你对这个问题和解决方案的信念是增强了还是减弱了？我可以告诉你，得到的答案各不相同。有些人会说：“哦，斯科特，我信念更坚定了。我学到了很多东西，从客户那里获得了验证，但我们还没找到正确的解决方案。这快把我逼疯了。我们尝试了三次，每个产品都失败了，但我的信念比以往任何时候都坚定。”（00:45:49）对于这些人，我会说：“你知道吗？你正处于混沌的中期阶段。坚持下去吧。这是正常的。” 但很多时候，我会听到：“说实话，如果当时我知道现在所知道的，我绝不会做这些事。天哪。”我会说：“那就退出吧。”人生短暂。你有一支出色的团队。转型吧。做些完全不同的事情。如果你失去了信念，在创业世界里，你就不该继续做现在正在做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sometimes, there are moments of that, I imagine. And so, there's probably some spectrum of just how little conviction and how long you felt that, right?
turns.zh: 有时候，确实会有这样的时刻。我想，信念的程度和持续时间可能存在某种程度的差异，对吧？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I think so. But at the same time, listen, we all have ups and downs. We all have good days and bad days. However, I do think that great founders are just... They absolutely know in their core that something needs to exist, and they will just be ruthless and relentless until it does. But if you lose that, I actually don't know if you have the fuel to continue. So listen, you're right. Don't make a bold decision on a bad day. But if the conviction generally dissipates, be open-minded about other options.
turns.zh: 我也这么认为。但同时，听着，我们都会经历起起落落，有好日子也有坏日子。不过，我确实认为优秀的创业者绝对知道某种东西必须存在，他们会不择手段、不屈不挠地去实现它。但如果你失去了这种信念，我真不知道你还有没有继续下去的动力。所以听着，你说得对。别在糟糕的日子里做重大决定。但如果信念普遍消退，那就对其他选择保持开放的心态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You do a lot of angel investing, talked to a lot of founders. What is it that you look for? What do you think is important for a startup to show you for it to feel like a good bet that it'll likely work out? What are some of the important attributes that you look for?
turns.zh: 你做了很多天使投资，接触过很多创业者。你寻找什么？你认为对一家初创公司来说，哪些方面能让你觉得它很有希望成功？你看重的关键属性有哪些？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I'll talk for a few things on team and then a few things on product.
turns.zh: 我会从团队和产品两个方面来谈谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: On team, I really value founders who listen, who really learn, who long to shake shit up a bit, and also value the mission that they're on more than the money that it yields because I do think that especially during a period of time where you don't have revenue, you're going to need to be motivated by something grander and bolder than revenue. (00:47:47): I also have an allergic reaction to founders that are real promoters who are constantly trying to sugarcoat the truth, who like to gloss over the hard parts. I've always admired leaders that are optimistic about the future but very pragmatic and somewhat pessimistic about the present. So the founders that I have a great sort of chemistry with are people who are like, "This is how big the market is. This is how amazing this is. I know this needs to exist." (00:48:15): But we've got a lot to figure out. There are things that are not working. We don't have these data sets. These are the major obstacles we're struggling with. These are the things that keep me up at night. Those are real people. And you know that in that volatile messy middle that they're going to inevitably go through that their team, their investors are going to have the real truth and they're going to be able to engage and find solutions. (00:48:37): So I really love finding those types of founders, and I'm very wary of the name-dropping overly promoting folks who are unlikely to be able to partner in that way. On the product side, I'm looking for an object model way of thinking about a product that I am confident the will scale and as they solve their problem. And when I say object model, what I mean is it clear whenever you're seeing the product, how it works, where you came from, where you're going? (00:49:11): Those are the three questions I always ask when I'm doing product reviews. It's like, "How did I get here? What do I do now? And what do I do next?" And I feel like every screen and every product experience, you should be able to answer those three questions. Sometimes, I'll be talking to a team that says they're design driven, says that they're building a incredible product, and they'll show me a demo and I'm like, "This is all over the place." There's no clean clear breadcrumbs and object model for how this thing works. How are they ever going to get people through their funnel? Clearly, they don't value this as a core principle, and that's also always a red flag. And then finally, I just obviously have to believe in the problem they're solving. So those are some of the things I think about.
turns.zh:
在团队中，我特别欣赏那些善于倾听、真正学习、渴望有所突破的创始人。更重要的是，他们对使命的执着远超对金钱的追求，因为我认为，在没有收入的初创阶段，创始人必须被比金钱更宏大的愿景所驱动。

（00:47:47）：我对那些虚伪粉饰现实、回避困难的创始人深感反感。我一直欣赏那些对未来充满乐观、同时又务实且对现状持悲观态度的领导者。因此，与我能产生强烈共鸣的创始人会这样说："这个市场的规模如此之大，这个想法如此惊艳，我知道它必须存在。"（00:48:15）：但我们还有许多难题需要解决。有些方案行不通，我们缺乏数据集。这些都是我们正面临的重大挑战，也是让我夜不能寐的难题。这些都是真实存在的挑战。在动荡混乱的过渡阶段，团队和投资者必须直面真相，共同寻找解决方案。

（00:48:37）：所以我特别欣赏这种类型的创始人，而对那些只会空谈、粉饰太平的人则保持警惕。产品层面，我寻找一种对象模型的思维方式——我确信这样的产品能随着问题解决而扩展规模。所谓对象模型，就是当你看到产品时，能清晰理解其运作机制、来龙去脉和未来方向。（00:49:11）：这是我进行产品评审时始终追问的三个问题："我是如何走到这一步的？现在该做什么？接下来又该怎么做？"我认为每个界面和产品体验都应该能回答这三个问题。有时，团队自诩设计驱动、打造惊艳产品，但展示的Demo却混乱无序，缺乏清晰的逻辑线和产品架构，又怎能引导用户完成转化路径？显然，他们没有将此视为核心原则，这也是一个危险信号。最后，创始人必须让我相信他们解决的问题的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you focus primarily on consumer or do you invest all over the place? And I'm asking in case people want to reach out and maybe, "Hey Scott, you want to [inaudible 00:49:59]."
turns.zh: 你们主要关注消费领域，还是投资领域广泛？我这么问是因为有些人可能想联系你，比如：“嘿，斯科特，你想[00:49:59未听清]。”

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Yeah. No. I'm pretty agnostic. I look for product design-oriented teams making things that need to exist. Beyond that, I try not to be too prescriptive.
turns.zh: 是的。不。我持开放态度。我寻找专注产品设计、致力于创造刚需产品的团队。除此之外，我尽量不做过多限制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Excellent. Any last words of wisdom that you think impact the way people build product in the world that tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of listeners listening? Is there anything else you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 好的。太棒了。你有没有什么智慧箴言，能影响全球数万、数十万听众的产品开发方式？在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Two quick things. One, for the moment that we're in, and then one for why we do what we do. For the moment that we're in, we're in a resource-constrained environment. Let's face it. We're all going to have less money, fewer headcount, all that kind of stuff. (00:50:35): And I've always found that resourcefulness brings you further than resources despite the fact that over the last seven to 10 years, we've basically thrown resources at every problem. Oh my gosh, this is not scaling. Throw more money at servers. Oh my goodness, we need more people on the social media team. Throw more money at headcounts. We've had a resources way of solving our problems as opposed to a, well, let's refactor how we run that database, or let's refactor how that team answers customer service requests. Let's bring a new technology to make it more efficient. Let's leverage and play with AI to see if that can help us. (00:51:11): We are in this era now where we're being forced to be resourceful and to refactor as opposed to hire and throw resources at problems. I think that's a great opportunity. I feel like this is where the best teams are going to build that muscle, that are going to go the distance. That's why all these VCs say it's so cliche that the best companies are always built in errors like these. (00:51:33): So my point number one is capitalize on the crisis, everyone. If resources are carbs, resourcefulness is like muscle. It stays with you. It makes you stronger, and it helps you have a better intuition and better performance over time. And then, I guess taking a step back, I would just encourage folks to recognize that anything amazing in the venture world is ultimately an exception. (00:52:05): And with all of the best practices, Lenny, that you and I just discussed and all the stuff that we read and books and whatever else, I always try to remind myself that at the end of the day, sometimes, exceptions are the rule when it comes to doing something truly transformative and that nothing extraordinary is ever achieved through ordinary means. And so, while we should always take these best practices and, sure, listen to some of the lessons I learned the hard way and whatever else, but at the same time if everyone says you're crazy, you're either crazy or you're really onto something. So take that with a grain of salt.
turns.zh:
两件小事。一是关于我们当前所处的环境，二是关于我们为何要采取当前行动。就当前环境而言，我们身处资源受限的局面。说实话，我们所有人都会面临资金短缺、人员减少等诸多挑战。（00:50:35）我一直认为，无论资源多么充足，足智多谋才能助你走得更远。过去七到十年间，我们总是用大量资源去解决每个问题。比如，天哪，这根本不是扩展规模啊！给服务器多加钱！天哪，我们需要更多社交媒体团队的人手！给人员增加预算！我们用资源堆积的方式来解决问题，而不是反思如何优化数据库运作，或者如何让团队更高效地处理客服请求。又比如，引入新技术提升效率，利用AI助力业务发展。

（00:51:11）如今我们身处这样一个时代——被迫发挥足智多谋、进行架构重构，而不是简单地砸钱雇人来解决问题。这种局面恰恰是绝佳机遇。我认为，最优秀的团队正是在这种挑战中锻炼能力、蓄力前行。这就是为什么所有风投都说，在危机中诞生的伟大公司往往是特例。

（00:51:33）所以我的第一点是：大家要善加利用危机。若资源是碳水化合物，足智多谋就是肌肉。它会伴随你一生，让你更强大，帮助你逐步提升洞察力和业绩表现。

（00:52:05）退一步说，我想提醒大家，创业界的任何奇迹最终都是特例。即便我们遵循了所有最佳实践，参考了你我探讨的经验、阅读的书籍等等，我始终告诫自己：归根结底，想要实现真正变革性的突破，常规方法往往行不通。当然，我们应该借鉴这些最佳实践，吸取我用血泪换来的教训，但与此同时，如果所有人都说你疯了，那要么你真疯了，要么你确实找到了正确的方向。对此，别太当真。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that. Speaking of extraordinary, I thought it'd be cool to just give you a chance to talk about what you're doing at Adobe. What are some of the products that you're working on? What should folks know about potentially what's happening in Adobe they may not be aware of?
turns.zh: 太棒了。说到非凡之处，我想借此机会聊聊你在Adobe的工作。你们正在开发哪些产品？对于Adobe正在进行但外界可能尚不了解的项目，人们应该了解哪些信息？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Yeah. No. Thanks for asking. For us, I would say there's really three trends that are driving or three waves of transformation, I would say, that are driving the strategy right now for us. One is just that people are becoming more creatively confident. It's kind of wild that we're like most confident as five-year-olds creatively when we're drawing and our parents are like, "Oh my God, that's beautiful. That's amazing. Let's put it on the fridge." And then creative confidence kind of goes down from there for most adults, and that's really sad. (00:53:22): And with generative AI and tools, we have something called the Adobe Express in market, and our generative AI offering is called Firefly. These types of tools make people feel more creatively confident right away. It's pretty amazing to see people that would never pick up a pen and draw or suddenly feeling confident. So I would say that's like wave number one. (00:53:42): Wave number two that we talked about a little earlier is the fact that creative professionals can now explore 10X the surface area of possibility. These tools are making them so much more efficient. And some people are like, "Oh my gosh, creative pros are going to be replaced." No. No, no, no. They're not. They're just going to find 10X better solutions. They're going to have that capability to explore more possibilities. And that's what makes design great, is finding, exploring more surface area. (00:54:10): And then, I would say the third wave that's fascinating to me is personalization. I think we talked about this a little bit, our apps will meet us where we are. I think that every marketing experience will be increasingly personalized for each of us. Every commerce experience, they'll know who we are. They'll just show us our shoe size and no one else's. (00:54:28): These sorts of transformations will really change the entire world of commerce, and content, and media, and everything else. And Adobe has a big digital marketing business that is focused on enabling some of that. So those are factors of strategy that I would say are driving some of the new products we have under development. And now, it's all about let's talk more shit.
turns.zh:
是的。不了。谢谢你邀请。对于我们而言，我认为有三个趋势或三大变革浪潮正在推动我们的战略方向。首先，人们正变得越来越有创意自信。说起来挺有趣的，五岁孩子在涂鸦时最具创造力，而父母们总是惊呼“天哪，太棒了！我们要把它贴在冰箱上”。但大多数成年人的创意自信感却在逐渐消退，这真的很令人遗憾。（00:53:22）  
借助生成式人工智能和相关工具，我们推出了Adobe Express等产品，生成式人工智能产品名为Firefly。这类工具能让人们瞬间重拾创意自信。看到那些从不拿起笔作画的人突然变得信心满满，真是令人惊叹。这就是第一波变革。（00:53:42）  
我们稍早提到的第二波变革在于，创意专业人士现在可以探索十倍于以往的可能性空间。这些工具极大提升了他们的效率。有人担忧“创意人才会被取代”。不不不，他们不会被取代。他们只会找到十倍优化的解决方案，获得探索更多可能性的能力。而这正是设计的魅力所在——不断探索更多可能性。（00:54:10）  
第三波变革最让我着迷——个性化。我认为我们之前讨论过这一点，未来我们的应用将精准服务用户。每个营销场景都将为我们量身定制，每个购物场景都能识别我们的身份，只向我们展示我们的鞋码，而非其他人的尺码。  
这类变革将彻底重塑商业、内容、媒体等领域。Adobe拥有庞大的数字营销业务，致力于助力实现这些变革。这些战略要素正是我们正在开发的新产品的驱动力。现在，让我们开始激烈的提问环节吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. You need a banner of that. It's been amazing to watch Adobe's rise over the last decade. It just felt like it was going nowhere. And all of a sudden, it's a juggernaut. And so, great work, Scott and everyone else involved. But with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. We'll try to go through it pretty fast. Sound good?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你需要把这句话做成横幅。过去十年间，Adobe的崛起令人惊叹。当时感觉它毫无进展，可如今已然势不可挡。Scott和所有参与其中的团队，干得漂亮。接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题，咱们尽量快速完成。同意吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Sound excited. Here we go.
turns.zh: 好。听起来很兴奋。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Sounds good. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的。开始吧。你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: First is Build by Tony Fadell. Tony is just an amazing, charismatic, deeply pragmatic, product builder. He's been brave enough to do both Adams and Bits as he says. And his book is just chock-full of wisdom. I do appreciate some of these kind of laws of nature, laws of power type books. I love psychology books. (00:55:47): I'm trying to think of some offhand that have really struck me. But understanding the natural human tendencies of people, I think the laws of power talks about tons of wars over centuries and what sorts of natural human tendencies or inequalities drove massive rebellions and revolutions. These sorts of insights, believe it or not, parlay into decisions we make in products and making people feel successful and productive. So I don't know. I love those books just because I think that they remind us of the limitations and opportunities or possibilities of humanity.
turns.zh: 首先是托尼·法德尔（Tony Fadell）的《Build》。托尼是一个极具魅力、务实的产物创造者。他曾勇敢地尝试打造Adams和Bits等产品，正如他所言。他的书中充满了智慧。我特别欣赏这类揭示自然法则、权力法则的书籍。我也热爱心理学著作。（00:55:47）：我正努力回想一些让我印象深刻的书籍。但理解人类的自然倾向，我认为《权力法则》探讨了几个世纪以来无数战争背后的深层人性法则，以及不平等如何引发大规模的反叛和革命。这些洞见，信不信由你，确实能启发我们在产品设计中如何让用户感到成功和高效。所以我不知道。我喜欢这些书，正是因为它们提醒我们人类的局限性和可能性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: What I love is these documentaries about the cosmos and about the edge of our understanding of black holes and what happens out there in space. So I don't remember. I know one is called Cosmos on Netflix. There are a few of them. But in my downtime, I get lost in some series like that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那些关于宇宙的纪录片，关于我们对黑洞认知边界的探索，以及太空中发生的种种奇观。我记不清了。我知道Netflix上有一部叫《宇宙》的。还有几部类似的作品。但在休息时间，我会沉浸于这类系列片中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have kids, one or more kids.
turns.zh: 你有孩子吗，一个或多个？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are you doing to help them plan for this future?
turns.zh: 你如何帮助他们规划未来？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I think about this all the time. What are our children going to do in a world where if you believe Vinod Khosla's prediction that 80% of the work, of 80% of jobs will be replaced by AI, what will people do? As we talked about their ingenuity will be unleashed, that's great. But ultimately, I always revert back to this one belief that if people are passionate, they become successful in something. (00:57:21): So I've always just been focused on trying to make sure that they find something they're super passionate about. And it doesn't even matter if the thing they find now is the thing they do later because I do believe that passion in itself and taking initiative on your passion is a muscle memory that once you develop it... I have a daughter who loves horseback riding. I don't know if she's going to do horseback riding forever or whatever. But I think that the passion that she has for it, and this desire to be better and to constantly learn more and do more, that in itself is like a replicable muscle memory. So I don't know what the future holds, but I believe that passionate people will always have a path.
turns.zh: 我一直在思考这个问题。当维诺德·科斯拉（Vinod Khosla）预测80%的工作、80%的职位将被AI取代时，我们的孩子将何去何从？正如我们之前讨论的，他们的创造力会被激发，这很棒。但最终，我始终坚信只要人们充满热情，就能在某个领域取得成功。（00:57:21）：所以我一直致力于确保他们能找到自己真正热爱的事业。即使他们现在找到的兴趣点并非日后从事的职业也无妨，因为我相信，热情本身以及为之主动付出的努力，就像肌肉记忆一样。一旦养成这种习惯……我女儿喜欢骑马。我不知道她是否会一辈子坚持，但我认为她对骑马的热情，以及不断提升自己、学习新技能的渴望，本身就是一种可复制的肌肉记忆。所以我不确定未来会怎样，但我相信有热情的人总能找到出路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that. What's a favorite interview question you like to ask when you're interviewing people?
turns.zh: 太棒了。在面试别人时，你最喜欢问的一个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: There's a real one, and there's a snarky one. So I do love trying to understand if people are introspective. And so, I like asking about something people have learned about themselves that reveal the limitation in how they work. It's a way to test introspection. And once this person hits their limits or struggles, can they be open and introspective or are they going to blame and point fingers? So I do ask that. I also like the question, like, "Do you consider yourself lucky?" I think it's a fascinating question because also some people who are super insecure about where they are and how they got there and might decline admitting luck, those who are comfortable should admit that they were lucky, I mean, I think the truth is we're all very lucky and certainly privileged. And I just think that that's always an interesting conversation.
turns.zh: 世上有两种人，一种是真正善于自省的，另一种则带有讽刺意味。所以我确实喜欢试着了解人们是否善于自我反思。比如，我会问他们从自身身上学到了什么，哪些东西暴露了他们的工作方式局限性。这是测试人们自省能力的一种方式。一旦他们遇到挑战时，是能保持开放和自省，还是会互相指责和推卸责任？这就是我会问的问题。我还喜欢问：“你认为自己幸运吗？”我觉得这个问题很有意思，因为有些人对自己的处境和成功之路心存不安，可能会否认运气的存在；而那些心安的人则会承认自己确实运气不错。我认为我们每个人都确实很幸运，甚至可以说享有特权。这总是一个很有趣的话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite reason product you've discovered, app or physical product? Anything that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 你最近发现了什么喜欢的优质产品吗？应用程序或者实体产品都可以？有什么想到的吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I've been playing with a product called Queue. And it's Q-U-E-U-E, I think. And it's basically a way to keep a queue of all of this content you want to watch across every streaming platform because there's so much content across so many streaming platforms and to make your own queue and then to see your friends queues and to see what content is in most of the people you know queues, it's actually an incredible graph of kind of stuff that people want to watch or have liked that I think we're going to need in this world where there is just a billion sources of content.
turns.zh: 我最近一直在玩一款叫Queue的应用。应该是Q-U-E-U-E吧。这款应用能帮你把想看的内容汇总到各个流媒体平台的队列里，因为现在流媒体平台内容太多，想找到心仪的内容实在太难了。你可以创建自己的队列，查看朋友的队列，还能了解他们最常观看的内容。这简直就是人们想看或喜欢内容的超大图谱，在这个充斥着数十亿内容源的世界里，它太有用了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm definitely going to check that out. I've been looking for an app like that of I'm sitting in the evening, "What the hell should I watch?" I've seen everything that exists on the internet. So that's awesome. What's a favorite AI tool that you've recently discovered or find useful that isn't something Adobe has made?
turns.zh: 我肯定会去试试看的。我一直在找这样的应用，比如晚上坐着无聊时想：“到底看什么好呢？”网上能搜到的内容都看遍了。所以这太棒了。你最近发现了什么好用的AI工具吗？不是Adobe出品的那种。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: Okay. Well, I will mention if it's okay a product that I did invest in.
turns.zh: 好的，如果你不介意的话，我可以提一下我投资过的一个产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然可以。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: But it's a product called Tome. And they can take a narrative that you want to put into a presentation, and with AI basically create just a draft of this presentation with imagery and compelling points. And it's almost as if you handed this off to an intern and said, "Come back to me with something I can work with." And suddenly, it's instantly there. So that's been like a fun one to play with.
turns.zh: 但这款叫Tome的应用特别棒。你可以把想放进演示文稿的叙事内容交给它，它会用AI生成带有图片和吸引人要点的演示稿。这就好像你把任务交给实习生，让他回头给你个能用的版本。结果一秒钟就出来了。玩这个应用特别有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I will check that out. We'll link to that. Also reminds me Kevin Kelly on Tim Ferriss was talking about how AI and ChatGPT is basically an intern. That's like the level of their skill right now. They're just this intern that's helping out with stuff.
turns.zh: 我会去看看的。我们会附上链接。这让我想起凯文·凯利在蒂姆·费里斯的节目里说过，ChatGPT和AI基本上就是个实习生。这就是它们目前的水平。

turns.speaker: Scott Belsky
turns.en: I think that's right. And that's why we have to see it as a resource but not a constraint because, again, it's answering that question like what would it look like if as opposed to doing true distinct thinking per se.
